title: Dependable Long-Horizon LLM Agents: A Trajectory-Centered Empirical Study of Where Errors Enter and Which Controls Reach Them
trick: Read each failed multi-agent run end to end and record where the wrong state first entered, who later saw evidence against it, and which control would have reached it, instead of a blame label.
framing_stripped: Called a 'trajectory-centered dependability framework' with an 'episode record', operational phases P0-P7, state domains R1-R6, dynamics H1-H7 and eleven 'control families' drawn from classical fault tolerance (Avizienis et al. 2004); it is (a) a 38-field annotation form filled in by one LLM instance (Claude) per trace for 95 failed runs taken from two public corpora (Who&When: 29 hand-crafted Magentic-One and 59 algorithm-generated CaptainAgent runs; MAD/MAST: 7 failed traces), reading each trace in full (sec. 3.2-3.3); (b) a comparison of the annotated fault origin with the corpus' human 'decisive step' on 88 Who&When runs (sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a); (c) a count of how often the trajectory already held evidence against the error and whether any agent used it (sec. 4.2); (d) a counterfactual judgement, per run, of which control family 'would have' observed and reached the episode and whether a local state restore would have sufficed (sec. 4.3, Table 4); and (e) one deterministic text scan over all 184 raw Who&When trajectories showing that 26 of the 58 hand-crafted runs end in a provider content-filter HTTP 400 after which the harness printed a FINAL ANSWER no agent produced (sec. 4.6).
method_equations: Task and trajectory (sec. 2.1): a task specification is $\mathcal{S} = (G, \mathcal{I}, \mathcal{A}, B)$ with outcome predicate $G$, required invariants $\mathcal{I}$, authorized actions $\mathcal{A}$ and resource budget $B$; a trajectory is $\tau = x_0, a_0, o_1, x_1, \ldots, a_{T-1}, o_T, x_T$ where $x_t$ is the partly observable agent-plus-environment state, $a_t$ an action and $o_{t+1}$ its observed result. Task completion means $G(x_T)$ holds; policy-compliant completion also requires $a_t \in \mathcal{A}$ for all $t$. A fault is a candidate cause of an error, an error a deviation in state, a failure a violation of the service specification. Episode record (eq. 1, sec. 2.4): $$E = \langle O, \mathcal{I}_E, \mathcal{L}, D, C, M, \sigma, U \rangle,$$ with origin $O$ (step, phase P0-P7, domain R1-R6, kind in {specification, fabrication, integration, decision, interface, environment, coordination}), affected invariants $\mathcal{I}_E$, dependency links $\mathcal{L}$ (each labelled with a dynamic H1-H7 and marked observed, intervention-supported or hypothesized), detections $D$, responses $C$, manifestations $M$, evaluation scale $\sigma$ and uncertainty $U$; the protocol expands this to 38 fields with fixed vocabularies, one primary episode per run (the earliest candidate fault whose consequences reach the final failure), every step-valued field anchored to a line of the normalized trace (sec. 3.2). Sample (sec. 3.3): 96 records out of 203 normalized traces (7 traces over 200,000 characters dropped), selected by annotation batch balanced on character count, 95 failed runs after excluding one MAD run with a correct answer; annotator self-confidence high 38, medium 55, low 2. Origin (Table 2, $n = 95$): by phase P0 13, P1 24, P2 34, P3 10, P4 9, P5 4, P6 1, P7 0; by domain R1 1, R2 71, R3 10, R4 2, R5 11, R6 0; the 10 P0/R5 cells are all CaptainAgent managers handing a garbled task to the group. Kind (Table 3): decision 40 (42%), fabrication 25 (26%), integration 10 (11%), coordination 8 (8%), interface 7 (7%), specification 4 (4%), environment 1 (1%). Position (sec. 4.1, Who&When): origin at median $0.18$ of run length; origin-to-symptom distance median $5.5$ steps (mean $17.9$, max $126$), $0.67$ of the run; against the corpus' decisive step on 88 runs, coincident in 40 (45%), within one step in 52 (59%), earlier in 37 (median 3 steps), later in 11, each of the 11 checked by hand; within-one-step agreement 66% on algorithm-generated vs 45% on hand-crafted runs. Dynamics (sec. 4.1): H2 contamination 74, H6 observability debt 44, H1 repeated exposure 38, H3 drift 36, H4 cascade 23, H7 budget exhaustion 18, H5 external impact 0 ('in 92 runs no action touched a shared or third-party system'). Evidence (sec. 4.2, Fig. 2b): contradicting observation or message before the symptom in 68 runs (72%), already present when the fault entered in 32; acted on in 7; in an agent's input and never mentioned in 41; explicitly acknowledged and continued unchanged in 19; so the unused share quoted as 88% is $(41 + 19)/68 = 0.88$, with the remaining run never seen by any agent. Detection and response (sec. 4.2): a deviation flagged in 29 runs (31%): erring agent or orchestrator 17, tool or verifier 9, another agent 3; uncertainty voiced only in 14 more; a response followed in 34 runs; responses that removed the deviated state: 0; partial removal: 4. Controls (Table 4; Primary = judged the most direct, Any = listed among reaching controls, multi-label): JUDGE (independent judge reading the unused evidence) 11 / 70 (74%); TC (task contract fixed at admission) 17 / 64 (67%); EVS (environment-verified state) 17 / 41 (43%); STALL (stall or termination rule) 14 / 38 (40%); PROV (provenance on stored facts) 20 / 36 (38%); HUMAN 0 / 31 (33%); POL (runtime policy) 3 / 30 (32%); TEST 8 / 20 (21%); COORD 4 / 18 (19%); IFS (information-flow separation) 1 / 4 (4%); CKPT (checkpoint/restore) 0 / 1 (1%). Restore reach (sec. 4.3): restoring the agent's own state to just before the origin would have sufficed in 35 runs; in 56 the fault sat in a plan, brief or stop rule that a restore would replay. Propagation (sec. 4.4): median 5 hops origin to symptom (range 2-8); state stays in one domain in 10 runs, crosses two in 42, three or more in 43; median distance by kind: decision 6 ($n = 35$), fabrication 5 ($n = 25$), integration 8.5 ($n = 10$); 72 runs end with a wrong output, 23 with no answer; a second causally independent fault in 34 runs (sec. 4.1), of which 8 are harness faults (sec. 4.4 counts 26 plus 8). By corpus (Table 5, % of each row's failed runs): Magentic-One $n = 29$: origin in P1-P2 52, fabrication 7, P0 0, evidence present 90, detected 41, median distance 18 steps, harness fallback 55; CaptainAgent $n = 59$: 66, 39, 20, 64, 25, 5 steps, 0; MAD $n = 7$: 57, 0, 14, 57, 29, not comparable, 0. Symptom labels (sec. 4.5, Table 6): 2.9 MAST modes per run; each frequent mode maps to 4-11 distinct origin (phase, domain) cells; mode 3.3 incorrect verification, assigned to 44 runs, has origins 16 decisions, 16 fabrications, 6 corrupted handoffs, 4 misread observations, 2 defective briefs (sec. 5); the P1/R2 cell is among the three most frequent cells of every one of the ten modes. Harness fault (sec. 4.6, deterministic scan of all 184 raw Who&When trajectories, independent of annotation): HTTP 400 from the provider's content filter on the orchestrator's progress-ledger call in $26 / 58 = 45\%$ of hand-crafted Magentic-One runs, 25 of which end with a harness fallback FINAL ANSWER, and in $0 / 126$ algorithm-generated runs; the corpus attributes those 25 runs to the orchestrator in 4 and to another agent (mostly the web surfer) in 21; recorded as a P6 termination fault in R3. Reporting formulas offered for others, not applied here (App. D.3, eqs. 6-7): for $n$ reset trials with $c$ successes, $\widehat{\mathrm{pass@}k} = 1 - \binom{n-c}{k} / \binom{n}{k}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{pass}^k} = \binom{c}{k} / \binom{n}{k}$, $k \le n$; verifier coverage $\mathrm{Cov}(\tau) = |\{o \in \mathcal{O}(\tau) : \text{check ran before its deadline}\}| / |\mathcal{O}(\tau)|$ with $\mathcal{O}(\tau)$ the set of applicable requirement-event obligations. No confidence intervals, no inter-annotator statistic, no intervention: all counts are of one LLM annotator's records (sec. 5.1).
load_bearing_assumption: That one LLM instance reading a whole trace under a four-page protocol locates the origin, judges whether evidence 'contradicts' a belief, and decides which control 'would have reached' the episode as a human expert would. The paper states the gap plainly: 'The records were produced by an LLM following a written protocol. We have no human inter-annotator agreement to report in this version' (sec. 5.1); 'we would not be surprised if it moved some of the kind labels, which were the hardest part of the protocol' (sec. 5.1); and on the control side, '"Would have reached" is a judgment about the trace, constrained by the control contracts of Table 10. It is not a measured intervention' (sec. 5.1). The two checks offered do not close it: agreement with the human decisive step within one step is 59% and the two labels 'answer different questions' by design (sec. 3.4), and the harness-fault scan is independent of annotation but speaks only to sec. 4.6. If the annotator systematically places origins early (it is instructed to find 'the earliest candidate fault whose consequences reach the final failure', sec. 3.2) or over-credits JUDGE because the protocol asks whether contradicting evidence existed, then 'faults enter at 0.18', '72% / 88%' and 'JUDGE reaches 74%' are properties of the protocol-plus-annotator, not of the agents. Second: that failure-conditioned corpora of sandboxed QA and coding runs (Who&When, MAD) say something about long-horizon dependability; the paper's own framework was 'partly built for' external impact (H5), which occurs in zero of 95 runs (sec. 5.1).
weakest_component: The annotation itself: a single LLM annotator per trace, no second annotator of any kind, no human audit of any subset, no kappa, on 95 runs selected by batch rather than at random (sec. 3.3, 5.1). Every headline except sec. 4.6 rests on it. The 'kind' labels that drive Table 3 and the mode-to-origin mapping of Table 6 are the ones the authors say were hardest; the 'evidence contradicts the belief' judgement of sec. 4.2 and the 'would have reached' multi-label of Table 4 are counterfactual readings with no ground truth, and Table 4 is explicitly 'contracts, not measured efficacy' (Table 10 caption). Next: (1) the 'most remembered' number, 72% of runs with contradicting evidence and 88% of those unused, has no denominator outside failed runs (a failure-conditioned corpus cannot say how often evidence is present and used in runs that succeed; App. D, Fig. 7 says so of this design in general); (2) the MAD arm is 7 failed traces after a 200,000-character cap, 'small and short-biased' (sec. 5.1), so the six-system claim is really two systems; (3) the harness-fault finding, the one result that does not depend on the annotator, is a string match for one provider error on one corpus split, and its headline count moves between 26 (crashes) and 25 (fallback answers) and the attribution split (4 orchestrator, 21 other) is 'of these 25', not of 26; (4) the 'restore would have sufficed in 35 runs' count is a judgement about a restore to 'just before the origin', which presupposes the origin was found correctly, the very field under question; (5) no cost, time or token figure for the annotation is given, so 'applied at scale' cannot be priced.
regime: Corpora: Who&When (Zhang et al. 2025b; 184 failed runs on GAIA and AssistantBench questions: 58 hand-crafted Magentic-One runs with orchestrator, web surfer, file surfer, coder and terminal agents; 126 algorithm-generated AG2 CaptainAgent runs) and MAD / MAST human-labelled split (Cemri et al. 2025; 19 traces from AG2, MetaGPT, ChatDev, HyperAgent, AppWorld, Magentic-One, OpenManus). Annotated: 29 hand-crafted + 59 algorithm-generated Who&When runs and 8 MAD traces (7 failed) = 95 failed runs; 7 traces over 200,000 characters dropped. Run lengths: Who&When sample median 33 steps (hand-crafted; corpus 32.5) and 9 (algorithm-generated; corpus 10); the running example is a 201-event TheAgentCompany log, 98 agent actions, 22 minutes, 81 turns of waiting (sec. 1, 2.2). Annotator: Claude (Anthropic), one independent instance per trace, protocol version 0.2 after a 20-trace pilot that surfaced 14 vocabulary gaps (sec. 3.2-3.3); agent models that produced the traces: unknown (not in text, inherited from the corpora). Tasks: question answering and programming in sandboxes; zero external mutations in the sample. Pass-rate band: not applicable (all runs are failures by construction). Annotation cost, tokens, dollars, wall time: unknown (not in text). Date: arXiv 2026-11-09, v1, cs.AI; venue: unknown (not in text); Villanova University ECE. Protocol, records and scripts: stated to be included as ancillary files.
information_asymmetry: (1) Label site vs trajectory. A Who&When label is one point, (responsible agent, decisive step); a MAST label is a symptom mode. The trajectory holds what neither carries: the earlier step where the wrong belief was first written into a plan or fact sheet (origin before the decisive step in 37 of 88 runs, median 3 steps; sec. 4.1), the observation that contradicted it (in 68 of 95 runs, in 32 before the fault was made; sec. 4.2), the path across domains (R2 to R5 to R3/R4, median 5 hops; sec. 4.4), and the provider HTTP 400 string that ends 26 of 58 hand-crafted runs before any agent answered (sec. 4.6). All of it is in the released text; the labels were assigned without it, and attribution models are trained and scored on those labels. (2) Run time vs hindsight. The evidence was not missing at run time: in 41 runs it 'was in an agent's input and was never mentioned', in 19 it was acknowledged and overridden, in one it was 'never seen by any agent' (sec. 4.2, by subtraction). Here the loss between agents is attention, not transmission. The scoring harness sees less than any agent: a FINAL ANSWER string, which in 25 runs it generated itself. (3) Annotator vs environment. The annotator reads the trace, never the environment, so 'would have reached' (Table 4) and 'restore would have sufficed' (35 runs) have no intervention behind them (sec. 5.1). (4) Failed-only vs population. Every rate is conditioned on failure; evidence use in successful runs, and content-filter crashes in runs scored as successes, sit unmeasured in the full corpora. Ideas come from (1) and (2): a deterministic harness-fault audit over every attribution corpus others train on (MAST-Data, LongRCA, TRAVERSE are unscanned), and a per-handoff ruler separating evidence lost in transmission from evidence delivered and ignored, which the paper's evidence field defines but reports only in aggregate.
occupies: Published: an episode-record schema (origin by phase P0-P7 and domain R1-R6 and kind, propagation dynamics H1-H7, evidence disposition, detection and response, reaching control families, restore reach, harness fault) written as a 38-field annotation protocol and applied by one LLM annotator to 95 failed Who&When and MAD runs; the counts that faults enter at median 0.18 of the run, mostly P1-P2 decisions or fabrications over task state (R2, 71 of 95), earlier than the human decisive step in 37 of 88 runs; that 72% of failed runs hold contradicting evidence before the symptom and 88% of those never act on it; that detection fired in 31% of runs and no response removed the deviated state; that an independent judge (74%), task contracts (67%) and environment re-verification (43%) reach most episodes while a checkpoint restore alone reaches 35 of 95; that MAST modes map many-to-many onto origin cells; and that 45% of hand-crafted Who&When runs end in a provider content-filter crash with a harness-generated final answer attributed by the corpus to a non-orchestrator agent in 21 of 25 cases. Not claimed and left open: any human annotation or inter-annotator agreement; any run with the controls in place; any corpus with external effects (tau-bench, TheAgentCompany) or with successful runs in the denominator; the same harness-fault scan on MAST-Data, LongRCA or TRAVERSE; and the effect of the 45% contaminated split on published attribution accuracies.

neighbors.title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
neighbors.trick: Collect 127 multi-agent systems' failed runs, have humans mark the responsible agent and the decisive step, and score attribution methods against those marks (best 53.5% on the agent, 14.2% on the step); this paper uses its traces, does not use its labels during annotation, finds its origin earlier than the decisive step in 37 of 88 runs, and shows 45% of its hand-crafted split ends in a harness crash the labels attribute to an agent.

neighbors.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
neighbors.trick: Build a 14-mode failure taxonomy (MAST) from 150 hand-read multi-agent traces, validate it with three annotators (kappa 0.88 on 15 traces, per this paper's App. D.2) and label 1,600+ more traces with an LLM judge; this paper takes 7 of its human-labelled traces, assigns its modes to all 95 runs (2.9 per run) and shows each mode maps to 4-11 different origin cells, so the mode does not say where a control would act.

neighbors.title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
neighbors.trick: Hand-annotate 1,794 Terminal-Bench trajectories from seven models and three scaffolds for when failure begins, how it evolves and whether it is recovered, finding epistemic errors that start within the first steps and stay hidden until unrecoverable; this paper cites it for 'first error early, symptom late' and differs by annotating multi-agent QA corpora with a control-reach field rather than single-agent coding runs.

neighbors.title: Locating Hidden Failures Makes Long-Horizon Agents More Reliable
neighbors.trick: Annotate 6,967 mistakes in 2,518 trajectories into 78 failure types (Traverse), show frontier judges find the first mistake in under a third of runs, and train a 4B verifier (Scout) that locates failures and selects among candidate runs at test time; this paper cites it for 'agents rarely catch their own mistakes' and positions its evidence-unused rate as the target such a verifier should read.

neighbors.title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
neighbors.trick: Treat the monitors that approve an agent's consequential action as a fail-prone system in the distributed-computing sense and show monitors sharing a base model or a poisoned evidence source fail together, so counting independent sources beats counting votes; this paper cites it for 'a verifier sharing the worker's information adds little' and uses it to argue the reaching control must read evidence the worker ignored.

theme_fit.why: directly a benchmark-validity and failure-attribution result: 45% of a public attribution split is scored on harness-generated answers mislabelled as agent faults, the human decisive step is downstream of the origin in 37 of 88 runs, and symptom taxonomies map many-to-many onto origins; the deterministic harness-fault scan is an instrument a solo first-year can run on every attribution corpus in a day

measures what is lost between agents and finds it is almost nothing in transmission: contradicting evidence was in an agent's input in 41 runs and acknowledged in 19, never seen by any agent in one; CaptainAgent managers corrupted the task brief at admission in 10 of 59 runs (P0/R5), and the common propagation path is belief (R2) to message (R5) to action; a per-handoff version of the evidence-disposition field is lane-shaped, but the paper does not measure compaction or memory cost

same words (credit, attribution, early fault, late symptom), different problem: no training, no RL, no credit signal; the origin-vs-symptom distance (median 5.5 steps, max 126) is at most a neighbour for step-level credit work

limitations_as_complaints: Every number I report except the harness scan comes from one LLM annotator per trace and nobody has checked it: 'The records were produced by an LLM following a written protocol. We have no human inter-annotator agreement to report in this version' (sec. 5.1); 'A human check of a subset is the obvious next step, and we would not be surprised if it moved some of the kind labels, which were the hardest part of the protocol' (sec. 5.1); my only external check is that 'our origins agree with the human decisive steps within one step in 59% of cases' (sec. 5.1), and the two labels 'answer different questions' (sec. 3.4).

My control-reach table is a reading of the trace, not an experiment: '"Would have reached" is a judgment about the trace, constrained by the control contracts of Table 10. It is not a measured intervention. Whether a control would actually have prevented a given failure requires re-running the agents with the control in place, which we have not done' (sec. 5.1); the table 'compares contracts, not measured efficacy' (Table 10 caption), so 'JUDGE reaches 74%' and 'a restore would have sufficed in 35 runs' are untested.

My corpora cannot show the failures my framework was built for, and my sample is neither random nor complete: 'Both corpora are question answering and programming in sandboxes. Not one run in our sample changes a shared or third-party system, so external impact (H5) and recovery of committed effects, which the framework was partly built for, cannot be studied here. That needs corpora like tau-bench or TheAgentCompany trajectories, or fault injection' (sec. 5.1); '96 annotated runs out of 203 normalized traces, selected by annotation batch rather than at random' and 'The MAD part is small and short-biased' (sec. 5.1); and every rate is conditioned on failure, so how often evidence is present and used in runs that succeed is not measured [paraphrase of App. D, Fig. 7: failure-conditioned corpora 'do not measure fault frequency'].
